Two indexes are declared in this document's metadata. Every mark below either
names one of them or files in the first, and every judgement this extension
makes about a mark — which entry it indexes, which target it resolves against,
which sort key it files under, which range it pairs with, and which other entry
it collides with once the LaTeX back-end has folded it — is made inside the one
index the mark belongs to. Each of those judgements is written wrongly here in
BOTH indexes, so this fixture is a document of mistakes rather than one to
copy: what it demonstrates is that the report names the index its judgement was
made in.

A mark that names no index files in the first declared one:
[Aardvark]{.index}. A mark that names the second files there:
[Babbage]{.index index="authors"}.

## A cross-reference resolves inside its own index

This target names a term the first index carries, and resolves:
[near]{.index entry="Neighbour" see="Aardvark"}. This one names, from the
second index, the same term the second does not carry:
[far]{.index index="authors" entry="Stranger" see="Aardvark"}. And this one
names, from the first index, a term only the second carries:
[remote]{.index entry="Outsider" see="Babbage"}.

## A sort key files a term in its own index only

The Hague files under Z in the first index, where a mark writes that key, and
under Q in the second, where a mark writes another: [Hague]{.index sort="Zebra"}
and [Hague]{.index index="authors" sort="Quebec"}. A second mark in each index
writes a rival key for the same printed entry, which the first key wins:
[Hague]{.index sort="Yankee"} and [Hague]{.index index="authors" sort="Romeo"}.

## Two entries print in one place and file under two keys

The index tool stores three levels, so an entry written deeper is folded into
its third. Two entries whose paths differ before the fold can be identical
after it, and a sort key written against the path the author wrote then files
the one printed entry twice. The first index writes that collision:
[Delta]{.index entry="alpha!beta!gamma!delta" sort="alpha!beta!Zed"} and
[Gamma, delta]{.index entry="alpha!beta!gamma, delta" sort="alpha!beta!Ada"}.
The second index writes its own, out of two different tails:
[Eff]{.index index="authors" entry="ada!bee!cee!dee!eff" sort="ada!bee!Wye"} and
[Dee, eff]{.index index="authors" entry="ada!bee!cee, dee!eff" sort="ada!bee!Vee"}.

## A range does not pair across two indexes

This opening is in the first index: [Cantor]{.index range="open"}, and this
closing is in the second: [Cantor]{.index index="authors" range="close"}.
Neither has a counterpart inside its own index, so each indexes as an ordinary
page number.

## Below the first index {#site-below-main}

Two marks stand below the first index's placement marker, and both still reach
their index. [Underwood]{.index} files in the first, whose entry file this
extension holds open past the place the index is printed;
[Ockham]{.index index="authors"} files in the second, whose own marker is
further down the page.

## Where the second index goes {#site-authors}

::: {.qi-index-here index="authors"}
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Below the second index {#site-below-authors}

[Vesalius]{.index} files in the first index and still reaches it, though it
stands below the second index's marker. [Petrarch]{.index index="authors"} is
below its OWN index's marker: the index tool closed that index's entry file
where the index was printed, so this term reaches no index at all, and the
extension says so.

## A second marker for the first index {#site-again}

The marker below names no index, so it is a second marker for the first one.
The first marker naming an index is the one that places it, so this marker
places nothing and the extension says so.

::: {.qi-index-here}
:::
